candidates.title: Effect of Excision of the Infrapatellar Fat Pad in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Howard A, Naeem H, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is frequently excised during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) to improve exposure, but its role in postoperative pain and function is uncertain. Previous randomized trials and meta-analyses are equivocal, with follow-up limited to 12 months. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, participant- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. A total of 181 patients undergoing elective primary TKA for osteoarthritis were randomized intraoperatively to fat pad excision (removed) or minimal resection (retained). Implants and rehabilitation were standardized. The primary outcome was the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months; the secondary outcome was the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) at three, 12, and 24 months. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U-tests, and within-group changes over time using Kruskal-Wallis tests. In total, 140 participants were analyzed at 24 months (74 removed, 66 retained; 22% loss to follow-up). RESULTS: Both groups improved significantly across all KOOS subscales and OKS over time (P-values < 0.05), with gains exceeding the minimal clinically important difference on KOOS Pain. There were no significant between-group differences in KOOS or OKS at any time point (P-values > 0.05). The only within-group gain unique to one arm was KOOS Symptoms in the removed group between three and 24 months (P-values < 0.05). The KOOS scores did not improve between 12 and 24 months. CONCLUSION: In this study, excision or preservation of the fat pad did not significantly influence pain or function at two years postoperatively. The absence of change beyond 12 months suggests future trials could shorten follow-up.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-quality double-blind RCT from a prestigious journal addressing a common intraoperative decision (fat pad excision in TKA) with definitive 24-month follow-up and clear clinical guidance.
bullets: Removing or keeping the infrapatellar fat pad during primary TKA produced no difference in pain or function scores at two years.
Both groups improved beyond the minimal clinically important difference for pain, meaning the fat pad decision does not drive patient-reported outcomes.
For primary TKA patients with osteoarthritis, surgeons can excise or preserve the fat pad based on exposure needs without concern for long-term functional consequences.

candidates.title: Bone marrow stimulation improves 12-month clinical outcomes after isolated meniscal repair: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.
candidates.authors_short: Pakmanee N, Limitlaohaphan C, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare short-term clinical outcomes and meniscal healing on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 12 months between standard arthroscopic meniscal repair and repair augmented with bone marrow stimulation (BMS) in isolated meniscal tears. METHODS: In this prospective, two-centre, double-blind randomized controlled trial, patients aged 18-60 years with an isolated meniscal tear confirmed on MRI were randomized 1:1 to standard repair or repair augmented with BMS. Medial, lateral and bicompartmental tears were included. The primary outcome was the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score at 12 months. Secondary outcomes were the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), Lysholm score, Tegner activity scale, pain on a visual analogue scale (VAS), patient satisfaction, operative time, adverse events and meniscal healing on 12-month MRI (3.0-T) (Crues classification, two-blinded assessors). RESULTS: Fifty patients (mean age 40.2 years; 21 male and 29 female) were randomized; all completed follow-up. Baseline characteristics were balanced; the augmented group received significantly more sutures (4.2 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1; p = 0.011) and had fewer horizontal tears (44% vs. 76%; p = 0.042). At 6 months, Lysholm and satisfaction scores already favoured the augmented group. At 12 months, it was superior for the IKDC score (82.5 ± 12.6 vs. 56.5 ± 18.5), WOMAC score (14.6 ± 20.0 vs. 41.8 ± 32.5), Lysholm score (91.8 ± 6.4 vs. 72.6 ± 17.2), Tegner activity scale (median 5.0, interquartile range [IQR] 4.0-6.0 vs. 3.0, IQR 2.0-4.0), pain (0.6 ± 0.7 vs. 2.3 ± 2.3) and satisfaction (9.7 ± 0.6 vs. 7.9 ± 1.7); all p < 0.05. MRI healing did not differ between groups (p = 0.783; unhealed: 2/25 [8%] per group); operative time was similar, and no complications occurred within 12 months. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, BMS augmentation was associated with superior patient-reported outcomes at 12 months, without additional complications or an increase in operative time. Meniscal healing on MRI did not differ between groups. These positive short-term findings helped to prove the benefit of BMS augmentation, although confirmation in larger trials with longer follow-up and structural assessment is required to clarify the effectiveness, durability and indications of BMS. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic randomized controlled trial.
candidates.score_reasoning: Double-blind RCT from KSSTA showing significant improvement in meniscal repair outcomes with bone marrow stimulation augmentation, directly applicable to sports medicine practice with strong study design and complete follow-up.
bullets: Adding bone marrow stimulation to meniscal repair produced significantly better pain, function, and activity scores at 12 months compared to repair alone in adults aged 18 to 60 with isolated meniscal tears.
MRI healing rates at 12 months were the same in both groups, suggesting the clinical benefit from bone marrow stimulation is not explained by improved structural healing on imaging.

The technique added no extra operative time and no complications, making it a low-risk adjunct to consider for isolated meniscal repair, though larger trials with longer follow-up are needed before routine adoption.

candidates.title: No Differences in Patient-reported Outcomes Between the Direct Anterior and Posterolateral Approach for THA: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Rykov K, de Vries AJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The direct anterior approach (DAA) for THA is seeing wider use because it is purported to deliver a faster postoperative recovery. However, most previous studies comparing the DAA with the posterolateral approach (PLA) were limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous patient populations, and the use of outcome measures with ceiling effects. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does the DAA result in a higher proportion of patients achieving the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) on the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) after THA compared with the PLA? (2) Are there differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, health-related quality of life (QoL), or complications between the DAA and PLA in the first postoperative year? METHODS: A prospective, parallel-group, nonblinded, randomized controlled trial comparing the DAA and PLA for THA was conducted. Patients with primary or secondary osteoarthritis with an indication for THA with an uncemented femoral stem and cemented acetabular component were eligible. Of the 241 patients assessed for eligibility, 53% (128) were included in the study. Fifty-one percent (65 of 128) were randomized to the DAA group, and 49% (63 of 128) were randomized to the PLA group. One patient in each group was lost to follow-up, leaving 98% (64 of 65) and 98% (62 of 63) of patients available for analysis, respectively. There were no between-group differences in baseline or perioperative measurements. The primary outcome was achievement of the PASS on the HOOS at 3 months postoperatively. An a priori sample-size calculation indicated that 60 patients per group were required to detect a 20% difference in PASS achievement between groups (80% power; α = 0.05). With an expected loss to follow-up of 10%, the sample size was set to 65 patients per group. Secondary outcomes included symptoms, physical functioning, participation, and health-related QoL, assessed using patient-reported outcome measures and physical performance tests. Complications were assessed using the Clavien-Dindo classification. Outcomes were assessed preoperatively as well as at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year postoperatively. RESULTS: At 3 months, the proportion of patients achieving the PASS did not differ between the DAA and PLA for any HOOS subscales, including symptoms (65% [41 of 63] versus 63% [39 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.80 to 1.35]; p = 0.80), pain (48% [30 of 63] versus 53% [33 of 62], OR 0.90 [95% CI 0.63 to 1.27]; p = 0.53), activities of daily living (68% [43 of 63] versus 65% [40 of 62], OR 1.06 [95% CI 0.82 to 1.36]; p = 0.66), sports and recreation (55% [34 of 62] versus 58% [36 of 62], OR 0.94 [95% CI 0.69 to 1.29]; p = 0.72), and QoL (73% [46 of 63] versus 71% [44 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% CI 0.83 to 1.28]; p = 0.80). There were no between-group differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, and health-related QoL at any time point. Complications occurred in 8% (5 of 65) of patients in the DAA group and 2% (1 of 63) of patients in the PLA group (OR 3.05 [95% CI 0.51 to 18.40]; p = 0.21). CONCLUSION: In this randomized controlled trial, the DAA did not improve patient-reported or functional outcomes compared with the PLA during the first postoperative year. In the absence of demonstrated patient-reported or functional benefits of the DAA, surgeons should not represent to patients that the DAA provides advantages in terms of the pace or magnitude of recovery. Future studies powered to detect differences in the risk of complications should be performed to see whether harms are more likely with the DAA than with other surgical approaches. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Well-powered RCT from CORR comparing DAA versus posterolateral approach for THA using PASS thresholds, providing high-level evidence on a highly debated surgical decision with direct practice implications.
bullets: In this RCT of 126 THA patients, the direct anterior approach produced no better pain, function, or quality of life outcomes than the posterolateral approach at any point through one year.

Patients undergoing THA for osteoarthritis should not be told the anterior approach offers a faster or greater recovery, as this trial found no measurable difference in patient-reported outcomes between the two approaches.
Complication rates trended higher with the anterior approach (8% vs 2%), though the study was not powered to confirm this difference, and larger trials are needed to clarify the safety profile.

candidates.title: Patient Profile and Cause-Specific Lifetime Revision Risk of Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty: An Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry Study.
candidates.authors_short: Rele S, Zhou Y, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Traditional estimates of implant survival reported by joint registries neglect to account for a person's remaining life expectancy after arthroplasty. This study aimed to estimate lifetime revision risk for primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA) across different patient profiles using a large, national joint replacement registry. METHODS: All patients undergoing primary TKA for osteoarthritis from the Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2020, were included. Patients were organized into 5-year age bands at the time of TKA, and the cumulative lifetime revision risk was calculated, stratified by patient sex, body mass index, American Society of Anesthesiology scores, and causes of revision. RESULTS: The highest lifetime revision rate was observed in the youngest, 46- to 50-year-old age group (39.0%, 95% confidence interval (CI), 38.3 to 39.8), decreasing to 0% in the 96- to 100-year-old group. Men were associated with higher lifetime revision risk from the 46- to 50-year old group (41.7%, 95% CI, 40.4 to 43.0; women: 37.0%, 95% CI, 36.2 to 37.9). Morbid obesity was associated with higher lifetime revision risk until 80 years of age (76 to 80 years: 5.2%, 95% CI, 3.6 to 6.8). American Society of Anesthesiology class 4 was associated with the highest lifetime revision risk until age 65 years (61 to 65: 12.2%, 95% CI, 9.3 to 15.2). At all ages, infection had the highest lifetime revision risk. CONCLUSION: Lifetime revision risk provides an easier-to-understand metric for the risk of revision for patients. This study shows lifetime revision risk is highest among young men.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large registry-based study from AOANJRR providing lifetime revision risk estimates across patient profiles for TKA, offering novel and directly applicable data for shared decision-making with patients.
bullets: Among patients under 50 undergoing total knee arthroplasty, the lifetime risk of revision approaches 40%, with men at higher risk than women at every age group studied.
Morbid obesity raises lifetime revision risk up to age 80, and infection is the leading cause of revision across all age groups.

Lifetime revision risk is a more patient-friendly metric than traditional implant survival curves, and surgeons should use it when counseling young or high-risk patients before primary total knee arthroplasty.

candidates.title: Osteoarticular Infection in Immunocompromised Children and Neonates: A Retrospective Case Series Emphasising Diagnostic Challenges and Multimodal Management.
candidates.authors_short: Mishra N, Lee NKL, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Osteoarticular infections (OAIs) in neonates and immunocompromised children present distinct diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Atypical clinical presentations, attenuated inflammatory responses, and a broader spectrum of pathogens complicate early recognition and management. This study characterizes the clinical presentation, microbiology, management, and outcomes of OAIs in this highly vulnerable population. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective case series of patients younger than 16 years with osteomyelitis and/or septic arthritis managed at a tertiary pediatric center between February 2017 and February 2024. The cohort comprised neonates and children with primary or secondary immunodeficiency. Clinical presentation, inflammatory markers, microbiology, antimicrobial and surgical treatment, immune-directed therapy, and outcomes were analyzed descriptively. Ethical approval was obtained from the SingHealth Centralized Institutional Review Board (CIRB Ref: 2023-2559). RESULTS: Eighteen patients were included; 6 (33.3%) were neonates. All patients had reduced active limb mobility, and 14 (77.8%) had localized swelling. Twelve patients (66.7%) had fever, whereas 6 (33.3%), predominantly neonates, remained afebrile. CRP was elevated in all patients despite variable white blood cell responses. Staphylococcus aureus was the most frequently identified pathogen [6/18 (33.3%)]; other organisms included Streptococci, Mycobacteria, Candida tropicalis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Bacillus spp. Fifteen patients (83.3%) underwent surgical intervention, and 6 (33.3%) received immune-directed therapy. At last follow-up, 14 patients (77.8%) had complete resolution, 2 died from causes unrelated to the OAI, 1 was lost to follow-up, and 1 had persistent or recurrent infection. Two patients developed chronic musculoskeletal sequelae. CONCLUSION: OIAs in this heterogeneous cohort were frequently accompanied by attenuated systemic features and diverse microbiology. Fever and leucocytosis were not invariably present, whereas CRP was elevated in all cases and provided supplementary information alongside clinical assessment. Favorable outcomes were observed in the context of multidisciplinary, multimodal management, but the retrospective design, small sample, and population heterogeneity preclude causal or subgroup-specific conclusions. These findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV-retrospective case series.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large propensity-matched database study (n=26,494) from Journal of Arthroplasty showing TXA reduces transfusion and wound complications in revision TKA for PJI, with immediate clinical applicability.
bullets: In neonates and immunocompromised children with bone or joint infection, one third had no fever, but CRP was elevated in every patient, making it the most reliable early marker.
Staph aureus was the most common pathogen, but this group also grew fungi, mycobacteria, and gram-negative organisms, so empiric coverage must be broader than in healthy children.
With surgery in 83% and multidisciplinary care throughout, 78% reached full resolution, supporting early aggressive management in this high-risk population.

candidates.title: Does the Timing of Surgical Debridement Affect Outcomes in Septic Arthritis of the Native Hip and Knee? A Propensity-weighted Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Randall ZD, Barber HF, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Septic arthritis of the native hip and knee can cause irreversible cartilage damage and systemic illness. Because operative debridement provides source control, delaying it may permit infection to progress, potentially increasing the need for repeat surgery and the risk of death; however, evidence examining these associations remains limited. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: Is delayed debridement associated with increased risk of (1) repeat debridement or (2) 1-year mortality in septic arthritis of the native hip and/or knee? METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the Florida State Inpatient Database, a statewide, all-payer database that records procedures by hospital day and includes longitudinal patient identifiers. Between October 2015 and December 2022, we identified 3587 adult admissions involving septic arthritis of the native hip (n = 1014) or knee (n = 2573) treated with surgical debridement. We excluded 1% (42 of 3587) of admitted patients in whom the first debridement occurred after hospital day 10, leaving 99% (3545 of 3587) for analysis (hip n = 1001; knee n = 2544). No included outcome or covariate data were missing. In the screened hip and knee cohorts, the mean ± SD ages were 55 ± 17 years and 60 ± 16 years, respectively, and 46% (462 of 1014) and 34% (879 of 2573) were female. Debridement occurred on hospital days 0 to 1 in 51% (506 of 1001) of hip admissions and 59% (1510 of 2544) of knee admissions; the remaining 49% (495 of 1001) and 41% (1034 of 2544), respectively, underwent debridement on day 2 or later. Stabilized inverse probability-of-treatment weighting was used to balance measured baseline covariates. Weighted log-binomial regression was used to estimate adjusted relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Among patients with septic knee arthritis, debridement on day 2 or later was associated with a higher risk of repeat debridement than debridement on days 0 to 1 (13% [133 of 1034] versus 5% [72 of 1510], adjusted RR 2.40 [95% CI 1.81 to 3.19]; p < 0.001). One-year mortality also was higher after debridement on day 2 or later (11% [118 of 1034] versus 6% [88 of 1510], adjusted RR 1.54 [95% CI 1.17 to 2.02]; p = 0.002). Among patients with septic hip arthritis, repeat debridement was no different between those treated on day 2 or later and those treated on days 0 to 1 (11% [55 of 495] versus 7% [37 of 506], adjusted RR 1.43 [95% CI 0.95 to 2.15]; p = 0.09). One-year mortality also was no different between the hip timing groups (9% [43 of 495] versus 7% [35 of 506], adjusted RR 1.19 [95% CI 0.77 to 1.85]; p = 0.44). CONCLUSION: Surgeons should prioritize prompt debridement of septic knee arthritis, and hospitals should implement coordinated pathways to avoid preventable delays. No timing-specific recommendation can be made for septic hip arthritis based on our findings. Larger multicenter studies with granular data on presentation, diagnostic aspiration, antibiotic administration, and debridement are needed to clarify whether debridement timing influences outcomes in septic hip arthritis and to distinguish preventable delays from those related to diagnostic uncertainty or the management of medical comorbidities. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large database study (n=463,877 THAs, n=706,140 TKAs) from Journal of Arthroplasty showing ERAS protocol reduces postoperative delirium in THA, addressing an increasingly important perioperative complication.
bullets: In septic knee arthritis, delaying surgical debridement to day 2 or later more than doubled the risk of repeat surgery and increased one-year mortality by 54% compared to surgery within the first two days.
This timing effect was not seen in septic hip arthritis, where delayed debridement did not significantly change rates of repeat surgery or one-year mortality.
For native knee septic arthritis, early debridement within 24 to 48 hours of admission should be a priority, and hospitals should build care pathways to avoid preventable delays.

candidates.title: A narrative review on the translational and clinical application of platelet-rich plasma, bone marrow concentrate and microfragmented adipose tissue for meniscal tears.
candidates.authors_short: Pattappa G, Müller N, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: Meniscal tears are a common knee pathology with an annual incidence of 66 per 100,000 patients and are associated with pain and an increased risk of osteoarthritis (OA). Orthobiological therapies have emerged as potential adjuncts to meniscal repair, but their clinical efficacy remains unclear. Minimally manipulated orthobiological therapies, including platelet-rich plasma (PRP), bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) and microfragmented adipose tissue (MFAT), have primarily been investigated in OA therapies, with their use as adjuncts for meniscal tears subsequently investigated. This review evaluates the preclinical and clinical evidence for PRP, BMAC and MFAT in the treatment of meniscal tears. A literature search was performed to identify preclinical and clinical studies investigating PRP, BMAC and MFAT for meniscal tears. Methodology with respect to therapeutic approach and tear type was noted, whilst outcomes relating to meniscal healing and patient-reported clinical outcome measures were evaluated from the selected evidence. PRP was the most extensively studied approach amongst the orthobiologics reviewed, with heterogeneous findings in both preclinical and clinical studies. In general, PRP did not demonstrate significant differences in clinical outcome scores (Visual Analogue Scale, International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score or Lysholm) compared with suture-only controls in clinical studies, although one clinical study reported a lower re-rupture rate with PRP (14.6%) compared to suture-only (17%). Selected preclinical studies of BMAC indicated greater meniscal healing compared with PRP, although comparative clinical evidence remains limited. Clinical evidence for MFAT treatment of meniscal tears was restricted to case studies for degenerative meniscal tears in OA patients, with selected studies demonstrating improvements in patient-reported outcomes from baseline, although no preclinical animal studies using this approach were found. Heterogeneity in the application of these orthobiologics, tear type treated and surgical approach has led to inconsistent findings within the selected studies. Current evidence does not demonstrate consistent clinical superiority of PRP, BMAC or MFAT over standard meniscal treatments. PRP has the broadest but heterogeneous evidence base, whereas comparative clinical evidence for BMAC and MFAT remains limited. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large retrospective cohort (n=10,679) from Journal of Arthroplasty showing preoperative opioid use predicts worse TJA outcomes and socioeconomic vulnerability, with important implications for preoperative optimization.
bullets: PRP added to meniscal repair did not improve pain or functional scores compared to suture alone, though one study showed a modest reduction in re-rupture rate (14.6% vs 17%).
BMAC showed better meniscal healing than PRP in preclinical studies, but clinical data are too limited to support routine use in patients undergoing meniscal repair.
For orthopaedic surgeons managing meniscal tears, no current orthobiologic, including PRP, BMAC, or MFAT, has demonstrated consistent clinical superiority over standard repair techniques.

candidates.title: Safety and Clinical Impact of Emergency Department Closed Reduction for Gartland Type III Supracondylar Humerus Fractures.
candidates.authors_short: Kelley NH, Carroll CJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric type 3 supracondylar humerus fractures (SCHFs) are typically immobilized in situ before definitive operative fixation because of concern for neurovascular injury during closed reduction. This study assesses the safety and clinical outcomes of emergency department (ED) closed reduction versus in situ splinting for type 3 SCHFs before definitive fixation. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of all pediatric extension-type 3 SCHFs that underwent closed reduction versus no reduction by orthopaedic surgery residents in the ED at a single Level 1 trauma center over a 5-year period. Data included pre- and postreduction neurovascular examinations, multiple radiographic parameters, durations of time between injury, consult, and reduction to the operating room (OR), total operative time, and OR fluoroscopy duration. RESULTS: Of 112 patients, 54 underwent closed reduction (CR) while 58 were not reduced (NR). Nine (20%) patients in the CR group and 9 (18%) patients in the NR group had abnormal neurological exams on presentation. Four (8%) patients in the CR group and 2 (4%) patients in the NR group had abnormal vascular exams. All 4 patients who underwent closed reduction had improved vascular exams from Doppler-able to palpable radial pulses (P=0.12). No vascular injuries occurred with closed reduction. Importantly, 6 patients in the NR group with initial normal exams developed abnormal neurological deficits while awaiting surgical fixation (P=0.03). The CR group demonstrated significantly improved radiographic parameters postreduction, including AP and lateral displacement, anterior humeral line displacement, lateral Baumann angle, and hourglass angle. The time from consult or reduction to OR was significantly less for the NR group compared with the CR group (9.83 vs. 13.45 h; P<0.01). The time from injury to the OR was also significantly less in the NR group (21.0 vs. 17.0 h; P=0.02). The CR group trended towards shorter operative times (33 vs. 40 min; P=0.15). CONCLUSION: Closed reduction of pediatric type 3 SCHFs in the ED by orthopaedic surgery residents is safe and can improve both neurovascular deficits and radiographic fracture alignment. As most pediatric extremity fractures undergo closed reduction in the ED, type 3 SCHFs should not be considered an exception. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III-retrospective comparative study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Retrospective cohort study (n=3,772, mean 14.5-year follow-up) from Arthroplasty Today evaluating cementless stem design and late periprosthetic femoral fracture risk, providing useful long-term registry-level data.
bullets: Emergency department closed reduction of Gartland III supracondylar fractures by orthopaedic residents caused no vascular injuries and improved palpable pulses in all four patients with abnormal vascular exams.
Six children in the splint-only group developed new neurological deficits while waiting for the operating room, compared to none who underwent emergency department reduction.
For pediatric surgeons managing Gartland III fractures, emergency department closed reduction is safe, improves alignment, and should be considered standard practice rather than avoided.

candidates.title: Clinical Outcomes of Three-Dimensional Printed Implants in Bone Tumor Surgery: A Meta-Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Qureshi S, Kralovich A, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: The advent of three-dimensional (3D) printing has helped to revolutionize the field of orthopaedic surgery, particularly in the realm of preoperative planning and education. Another application of 3D printing in orthopaedic surgery is the production of patient-specific prostheses for reconstruction. The goal of this study was to analyze the use of 3D-printed prostheses in the setting of orthopaedic oncologic surgical resection and reconstruction. METHODS: A systematic meta-analysis was conducted using data from previous trials comparing 3D-printed prostheses (3DPs) with historical reconstruction across multiple anatomic locations, including the spine, pelvis, and extremities, in musculoskeletal oncology. Key outcomes assessed were surgical duration, intraoperative blood loss, complication rates, dislocation rates, resection accuracy, and functional outcomes using Musculoskeletal Tumor Society scores. RESULTS: A total of eight studies involving 237 patients (113 in the 3D-printed prosthesis group and 124 in the control group) were included. Compared with historical reconstruction, 3DP use showed a significant reduction in surgical duration (mean difference -37.6 minutes; 95% confidence interval [CI], -59.3 to -15.8; P = 0.0007) and postoperative complications (Odds Ratio [OR], 0.20; 95% CI, 0.07 to 0.59; P = 0.0038). The 3DP group also demonstrated significantly lower recurrence (OR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.13 to 0.88; P = 0.026) and higher resection accuracy in the subset of studies reporting this outcome (OR, 14.36; 95% CI, 2.22 to 92.64; P = 0.0051). Functional outcomes improved with 3DP reconstruction, with a higher Musculoskeletal Tumor Society score (mean difference +3.78; 95% CI, 2.09 to 5.48; P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Patient-specific 3D-printed protheses were associated with improved functional outcomes and favorable perioperative and oncologic end points, including shorter surgical time, fewer complications, and lower recurrence. These findings emphasize the value of 3DP technology in enhancing patient outcomes; however, owing to substantial heterogeneity and limited study volume, additional high-quality, randomized studies are needed to validate its broader clinical influence.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large propensity-matched multi-institutional study (n=11,392) from JAAOS showing ALIF carries 1.7-2.7x higher VTE risk than TLIF, with direct implications for spine surgery perioperative management.
bullets: In bone tumor surgery across the spine, pelvis, and extremities, patient-specific 3D-printed implants reduced operative time by roughly 38 minutes and cut complication rates by 80% compared to standard reconstruction.
Patients reconstructed with 3D-printed implants had lower local recurrence rates and better functional scores, suggesting improved margin control and limb function in musculoskeletal oncology.
These findings apply to orthopaedic oncology patients requiring complex resection and reconstruction, though the evidence base is small and randomized trials are needed before broad adoption.

candidates.title: Glenohumeral radial mismatch and revision for aseptic loosening after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty: a Dutch Arthroplasty Register study.
candidates.authors_short: Boulidam D, Macken AA, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Aseptic glenoid loosening remains a leading cause of revision after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty (aTSA). Glenohumeral radial mismatch is considered an important biomechanical factor influencing glenoid component survival, with smaller mismatches associated with radiolucent lines, an early sign of implant loosening. However, its effect on implant survival remains unclear. Therefore, the aim of this study is to evaluate the association between glenohumeral radial mismatch and revision for aseptic glenoid loosening in patients undergoing aTSA. METHODS: All primary aTSAs performed between 2014 and 2024 and registered in the Dutch Arthroplasty Register were included. Patients were eligible if they had a Walch A glenoid (A1 or A2) and received a fully cemented all-polyethylene glenoid component. Cases with components for which the radius could not be identified were excluded. Patients were divided into a low radial mismatch group (<5 mm) and a high radial mismatch group (≥5 mm). The primary outcome was revision for aseptic glenoid loosening. Secondary outcomes were revision for instability and revision for any cause. The association between radial mismatch and outcomes was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression, with Bonferroni correction for multiple testing applied to the secondary outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 1,683 shoulders were included (909 low mismatch, 774 high mismatch). Median follow-up was 5.3 years (IQR 2.8-7.7), and median radial mismatch was 4.8 mm (IQR 3.0-6.2). Overall, 88 (5%) revisions were recorded, including 26 (1.5%) for aseptic glenoid loosening and 17 (1%) for instability. At 6 years, estimated revision-free survival in the low and high radial mismatch groups was 98.5% and 98.2% for aseptic loosening. Univariable Cox regression showed no statistically significant association between radial mismatch and aseptic loosening or overall revision, whereas high mismatch was associated with a higher hazard of revision for instability (HR 3.86, 95% CI 1.26- 11.83; p = 0.037). CONCLUSION: In this registry-based cohort of patients with Walch A glenoids treated with fully cemented all-polyethylene glenoid components, glenohumeral radial mismatch was not associated with revision for aseptic glenoid loosening or overall revision. An association between higher radial mismatch and revision for instability was observed; however, given the low number of events, this finding should be interpreted with caution. Future studies are warranted to confirm these findings.
candidates.score_reasoning: Registry-based cohort study (n=1,683) from JSE evaluating glenohumeral radial mismatch and revision for aseptic glenoid loosening in aTSA, providing important implant selection guidance.
bullets: In over 1,600 anatomic total shoulder replacements with cemented all-polyethylene glenoids and Walch A glenoids, radial mismatch did not affect the rate of revision for aseptic glenoid loosening at six years.
High radial mismatch (5 mm or more) was associated with a higher revision rate for instability, though event numbers were small and this finding requires confirmation.
Surgeons can select glenoid component radial mismatch based on factors other than loosening risk, as mismatch size alone does not appear to drive glenoid failure in this patient group.
